title: Share what helps
hookLine: Lohicca thinks a good discovery should be kept to oneself; the Buddha disagrees

cards: You find something that really helps: a way to sleep better, a way through grief, a habit that calms you down. Do you tell people? Or do you think: everyone has to find their own way, what can one person do for another?

The brahmin Lohicca, of the village of Salavatika, holds the second view, firmly. If a teacher discovers something good, he believes, they should keep it to themselves. Teaching others is just making new ties.
So when he hears the Buddha is nearby, he sends his barber, Rosika, with a dinner invitation.

teach.b: On the way, the barber walks beside the Buddha and quietly asks a favor: please free my master from this view. At the meal, the Buddha asks Lohicca directly. Is it true you think this?
Yes. So the Buddha asks about Lohicca's own life.
You live off the revenue of Salavatika, granted by the king. Suppose someone said Lohicca should keep all of it for himself and share nothing with the people who depend on him.
Would that person be helping those people, or endangering them? Endangering them, says Lohicca. Would that person have their welfare at heart?
No. Then, the Buddha says, it's the same with your view. Someone who says a good discovery shouldn't be shared puts an obstacle in front of everyone who could have been helped by it.
The Pali word underneath is anukampa, compassion: does such a person have others' welfare at heart?
Keeping good things to yourself, he suggests, falls short of it. Then he adds a careful distinction.
Some teachers deserve criticism: those who teach without having reached the goal themselves, and those whose students don't listen.
And one teacher deserves none: someone who has truly found something good and shares it so that others reach it too. So sharing isn't preaching at everyone.

It's not hoarding what genuinely helps. Lohicca's response is vivid. You've done for me, he says, what a man would do if he grabbed someone by the hair who was falling off a cliff, and set them on solid ground.

how: In Buddhist traditions, giving the teaching (dhamma-dana) is called the highest gift; teachers share it freely, and lay people support the printing and distribution of texts as an act of generosity.

o: a vow to keep good teachings private
a teacher's fee for sharing wisdom

games.q: share what helps: tap the pairs.
p: thought discoveries should be kept quiet
the barber who asked a favor

s: the barber asks the Buddha to free his master from the view
Rosika asks quietly on the way to the meal.
the Buddha says every kind of teacher deserves praise
he names teachers who deserve criticism, and one who doesn't: someone who has truly found the good and shares it.
Lohicca compares the Buddha's help to being pulled back from a cliff
grabbed by the hair as he was falling, and set on solid ground.

games.q: you're the Buddha at Lohicca's table. he believes good discoveries should never be shared. how do you reach him?
o: ask about hoarding the revenue of his own village.
games.why: the Buddha starts from Lohicca's own life: would keeping all of Salavatika's revenue for himself help the people who depend on him? Lohicca sees it at once.

practice: Think of something that has truly helped you, not something to sell anyone on: a practice, a book, a kindness, a way of seeing.
Bring to mind one person who might need it, picture telling them simply, with no pressure, and let a little warmth toward them rise.

wordCard.voice: Anukampa. A good discovery kept to yourself is a gift withheld; shared with compassion, it can pull someone back from the edge. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit anukampa: compassion, sympathy. the Buddha asks whether a hoarder has compassion for those who depend on him.

carryVoice: Your line: set them on solid ground. What helped you can help someone else. See you tomorrow.
